claims.text: Tribo-induced formation of a continuous protective oxide layer is the primary mechanism governing wear resistance in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings.
The kinetics of protective oxide-layer formation are directly modulated by alloy composition.
The initial material is an as-deposited, disordered, multi-principal-element HEA coating.
Changing the concentration of an oxide-forming element such as Ti provides a controlled intervention.
Ti is an oxide-forming element that influences phase-transformation kinetics in the proposed coating.
Tribological stresses under sliding can trigger oxide formation at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures.
Wear produces a fine, continuous protective oxide layer at the coating surface.
Changing oxide-forming-element content alters the kinetics of tribo-induced phase transformations.
An optimized concentration of the oxide-forming element promotes rapid formation of a continuous oxide scale during sliding.
Formation of a protective oxide scale minimizes material removal and enhances wear resistance.
Formation of the protective oxide scale lowers the coefficient of friction.
Relative to the baseline, the modified composition will form a more coherent and thicker protective oxide layer.
Relative to the baseline, the modified composition will have a lower friction coefficient and reduced wear volume.
The proposed behavior holds from room temperature through moderately elevated sliding temperatures while oxide-formation kinetics remain active.
In CrMnFeCoNi, the identity of the alloying elements affects oxidation behavior, with Mn acting as the major oxide-forming element and producing non-protective oxides.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits either increasing or decreasing the oxide-forming element, yet the prediction assigns improved oxide coherence, thickness, friction, and wear to the modified composition without specifying which direction or concentration is expected to be optimal.
